text: With a smaller head start, or a variable rate that starts higher, more stretches cost more in both halves, and the worst gets bigger. At every head start tested, the worst stretch began in April nineteen seventy-seven. And at every head start tested, some of the starts from nineteen fifty-four to nineteen eighty still cost more. So, back to the question: how much lower does a variable rate have to start before the risk has been worth it? Measured as how often it cost more in total interest than the nine percent fixed loan, and how much more at worst, history gives two answers. From nineteen eighty-one on, a two point head start was enough every time; from nineteen fifty-four to nineteen eighty, even three points was not, and the worst still cost six thousand thirty-three dollars more. Which kind of history comes next is something no replay can show.
